claims.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys are intended for service at high or ultrahigh temperatures.
The initial polycrystalline refractory HEAs have near-equilibrium microstructures.
The initial refractory HEAs exhibit significant lattice distortion.
The initial refractory HEAs have a low precipitate volume fraction.
A controlled series should vary precipitate volume fraction while keeping bulk composition and lattice distortion similar.
Increasing the nanoscale precipitate volume fraction at constant lattice distortion and composition increases yield strength in refractory HEAs.
Nanoscale precipitates increase yield strength by pinning or obstructing dislocations.
Nanoscale precipitates create local variations in elastic modulus.
Nanoscale precipitates perturb local phonon characteristics.
Precipitate-induced phonon perturbations alter the temperature dependence of elastic modulus.
Precipitate-induced phonon perturbations alter thermal expansion behavior.
At temperatures of at least 700 K, higher-precipitate samples will have greater yield strength than low-precipitate baseline samples.
At temperatures of at least 700 K, higher-precipitate samples will exhibit a more pronounced temperature dependence of elastic modulus than the baseline.
Moderate-to-high stress at temperatures of at least 700 K defines a regime in which thermally activated dislocation processes prevail.
Controlling the atmosphere to minimize interstitial impurities is important because impurities can alter microstructural evolution and mechanical properties during high-temperature aging.
Lattice distortion can affect shear modulus, dislocation structure, and plastic-zone development in refractory HEAs.
The magnitude of strengthening and thermoelastic changes depends on precipitate morphology.
The magnitude of strengthening and thermoelastic changes depends on alloy-specific interactions.
